desc:
A sequence a is defined by d = coefs.length initial terms a[0..d-1] = init and, for every index i ≥ d,

a[i] = coefs[0]*a[i-1] + coefs[1]*a[i-2] + ... + coefs[d-1]*a[i-d], all taken modulo 1,000,000,007.

Return a[n]. The index n can be as large as about two billion, so you cannot generate the terms one by one.

Example: coefs = [1, 1], init = [0, 1] is the Fibonacci sequence, so n = 10 gives 55.
hints: For small n you just iterate the recurrence. Why is that too slow when n is about 2·10<sup>9</sup>?
The window of the last d terms is a vector, and one step of the recurrence multiplies that vector by a fixed d × d matrix.
So the window after n - d + 1 steps is the matrix to that power times the starting window. Compute the matrix power by repeated squaring, with every product reduced modulo 1,000,000,007.
editorial: Write the state as the vector v_i = (a[i], a[i-1], ..., a[i-d+1]). The recurrence says v_{i+1} = T · v_i where the first row of T is the list of coefficients and the remaining rows shift the window down (a sub-diagonal of ones). Starting from v_{d-1} = (init[d-1], ..., init[0]) we get v_n = T^(n-d+1) · v_{d-1}, and a[n] is the first component.

If n < d the answer is simply init[n]. Otherwise raise T to the power n - d + 1 by binary exponentiation: about 31 squarings and at most 31 extra multiplications of d × d matrices, each O(d3). Total O(d3 log n) time and O(d2) space. Products of two residues reach about 1018, so Python integers are fine but fixed-width languages need 64-bit unsigned arithmetic or careful reduction. (Kitamasa's polynomial method improves this to O(d2 log n), which is overkill here.)
